title: Column Subtractor
context: Grade 5, the pages on subtracting decimals. An adult sees the steps of adding run again. What the pages are doing is taking away place by place with the greater number on top and the points in one line, trading across the point where a place is short. A mistaken addition is undone by taking the number away, and the wanted subtraction takes it away again.

writeup.why: Subtract decimals, from whole numbers too, with the points in one line and trading where a place is short, read the three wordings of subtraction, and undo a mistaken addition in two steps.
writeup.look: A column frame with one fixed point line, two cards lined up on it, trades drawn in vermilion above the columns, and a Wording card and an Undo panel on the later phases.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Column Subtractor' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x sixty-four, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many trades have been made, one for each block broken into ten. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x sixty-four, y 202. The frame spans x 110 to x 900 from y 230 to y 560, five columns 140 across headed Tens, Ones, Tenths, Hundredths and Thousandths, with the near-black point line at x 400. The two cards sit at y 300 and y 380, deep blue and labelled Given; the Top check outline lights amber around the upper card until it holds the greater number. A trade is drawn above its columns at y 250: one block of the left column breaks into ten small blocks of the short column, in vermilion, labelled Trade, and the top digits are rewritten there in small vermilion figures. The part taken away fades rose, labelled Taken away, and the difference is written green under a ruled line at y 500, labelled Difference. The Wording card sits at x 960, y 230, and the Undo panel at x 960, y 420, each 170 wide, stepping through its two steps one under the other. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across with a point key, for setting a decimal with up to three places or typing a difference into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. A decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it. The result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum, a difference or what is left, is green, with its shaded parts. Ten of one place traded for one of the next, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written after the point to line decimals up is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded part stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the decimal point is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label, Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left or Place holder, before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last difference in the frame, every trade still in vermilion above its column.

On the first two phases the two cards wait in the tray with the Top check unlit, and on the second the upper card is a whole number with no point. On the third the Wording card shows its three wordings. On the fourth the Undo panel shows the mistaken answer. source_tool.description: A column frame fills the working area: five columns headed Tens, Ones, Tenths, Hundredths and Thousandths around one fixed near-black point line, with an answer row under a ruled line. Two deep blue decimal cards labelled Given drag into the frame and slide until their points sit on the point line; a Top check lights the upper card amber until it holds the greater number, and the frame will not subtract before. A whole number card has no point until a Point first button writes a violet point after its ones digit and violet zeros after it, labelled Added zero. A Take button works one column at a time from the right, lit amber. When the top digit is too small, a tap on the column to its left breaks one of its blocks into ten of the short place, drawn in vermilion and labelled Trade, and the top digits are rewritten above in small vermilion figures; a trade from the ones crosses the point line. The part taken away fades rose, labelled Taken away, and the difference is written green in the answer row, labelled Difference. On the third phase a Wording card shows the same subtraction as subtract from, take away and how much less, and a tap on each lights which number goes on top. On the last phase an Undo panel takes the added number away once, back to the start, and once more for the subtraction that was wanted. A number pad sets any decimal with up to three places. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many trades have been made.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: strips cut into ten equal parts, hundred grids of ten rows and ten columns, place value charts with a column for each place, column sums with their points in one line, and measuring jugs, ropes and scales marked in tenths.

Every whole is drawn the same size as every other whole it is compared or combined with, and its parts are exactly equal: a strip in tenths has ten parts of one width, and a hundred grid is always a full ten by ten.
The decimal point is drawn large and always sits between the ones and the tenths. In a column, every point lies on one vertical line.
A place value chart names every column above its digit: Hundreds, Tens, Ones, the point, Tenths, Hundredths, Thousandths.
Where shaded cells are counted, exactly the stated number is shaded, and they stay countable at a glance.

Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a strip cutting into tenths, ten tenths sliding together into one whole, a zero appearing after the point, or a carry moving to the next place.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit or a part the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a decimal plays in a piece of working: every decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it, and every result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum or a difference, is green, with its shaded parts; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Ten of one place traded for one of the next place, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written at the end, after the point, to make like decimals is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey. An unshaded part of a whole stays warm white inside its outline, and the decimal point itself is near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.

phase_map.concept: Taking a decimal from a whole number
Three ways to ask for a difference

placement.where: After the class has measured two pencils and taken the shorter length from the longer on paper. The tool is what breaks one block into ten at every trade, and what runs a mistaken addition backwards in two steps.

answer_key.rule: Put the greater number on top, with the points in one line. Subtract place by place from the right. When a place is short, trade 1 of the place to its left for 10 of this place; it works across the point too. A whole number gets its point and zeros before anything is taken from it. Subtract 2.5 from 8.1, take away 2.5 from 8.1, and how much less 2.5 is than 8.1 all ask for 8.1 - 2.5. A number minus itself is 0. A mistaken addition is undone by taking the number away, and the subtraction that was wanted takes it away again, so it is taken away twice.
answer_key.wrong: The two cards are lined up again and the columns are worked one at a time from the right, every trade broken into ten in vermilion, with the child's difference kept in a row beside the answer row. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Write 8.3 as 8.30 and put the greater number on top, points in one line.
Hundredths: 6 cannot be taken from 0, so trade 1 tenth for 10 hundredths, and 10 - 6 = 4.
Tenths: 2 are left, and 5 cannot be taken from 2, so trade 1 one for 10 tenths, and 12 - 5 = 7.
items.question: What is 8.3 - 4.56?
items.checkpoint: When a place is short, trade 1 of the place to its left for 10 of this place.
items.misconception: Taking the smaller digit from the larger in each column, 6 - 0 and 5 - 3, which gives 4.26 instead of trading.

steps: Write 7 as 7.00, with its point after the 7.
Trade 1 one for 10 tenths, then 1 tenth for 10 hundredths.
That leaves 6 ones, 9 tenths and 10 hundredths to take from.
items.question: What is 7 - 2.45?
items.checkpoint: A whole number gets its point and zeros before anything is taken from it.
items.misconception: Lining the 7 up under the 5 of 2.45, which takes 2.45 from 7 hundredths instead of 7 ones.

steps: Take away 1.8 from 6.25 starts at 6.25 and takes 1.8 away, so 6.25 goes on top.
Subtract 1.8 from 6.25, and how much less 1.8 is than 6.25, ask for the same difference.
Tenths: 8 cannot be taken from 2, so trade 1 one for 10 tenths, and 12 - 8 = 4.
So 6.25 - 1.80 = 4.45. A number minus itself is 0, as in 3.72 - 3.72 = 0.
items.question: Take away 1.8 from 6.25.
items.checkpoint: Subtract from, take away and how much less all ask for the same difference.
items.misconception: Putting 1.8 on top because it is named first in the question, which makes the frame refuse to start.

steps: First undo the mistake: 7.9 - 1.6 = 6.3, the starting number.
Then do the subtraction that was wanted: 6.3 - 1.6 = 4.7.
items.question: Someone added 1.6 to a number instead of subtracting it, and got 7.9. What is the right answer?
items.checkpoint: A mistaken addition is undone by taking the number away, then taking it away again.
items.misconception: Taking 1.6 away only once, which gives 6.3, the starting number and not the answer.

items.question: What is 6.4 - 2.15?

teaching_notes: The greater number goes on top, with the points in one line. When a place is short, trade one of the place to its left for ten of this place, across the point too, and say each trade aloud. A whole number gets its point and zeros before anything is taken from it. Subtract from, take away and how much less all ask for the same difference; say which number starts on top.
